transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2029-03-06
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Aurora CTO), Liam O'Reilly (Platform Lead), Sara Gomez (ML Eng)

Summary:  (auto) High-level discovery on p95 latency targets, burst concurrency and streaming token/sec expectations for Aurora's "StreamBurst" feature. Customer evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) placements, needs baseline token/sec benchmarks and fallback/quantization strategies.

Topics: p95 targets, concurrency patterns, streaming vs batched calls, token/sec benchmarking, private deployment constraints (VPC/KMS), SOC2/compliance, cost tradeoffs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: All right, hey team, thanks for making time. I'm Maya from Redwood - AE - and with me is Diego, our solutions engineer. Could you quick introduce the Aurora folks?
[00:18] Priya Nair: Yeah hi, Priya here, CTO. We're trying to size StreamBurst which is our low-latency streaming inference layer, and want to figure out the best way to run it — hosted, dedicated, or VPC/private.
[00:32] Liam O'Reilly: Liam, platform eng. Main ask: p95 under production bursts, we see spikes to 600 concurrent streams, avg message length ~ 120 tokens but with long tails to 1.2k tokens. p95 target is 180ms for streaming chunks.
[00:47] Diego Ramos: Thanks, Liam. That p95 180ms is for chunk delivery or end-to-end? Can you clarify?
[00:53] Liam O'Reilly: Good point — that's for the chunk-level streaming p95, so per token/chunk emission when streaming; end-to-end response time can be higher.
[01:05] Sara Gomez: Also we do bursts where token/sec per stream jumps to 80-120 tokens/sec for tens of seconds, then back down. We need to understand token/sec headroom and multi-tenant isolation.
[01:20] Maya Chen: Great, that's clear. Diego, can you walk through how Redwood handles streaming and p95 targets across hosted/dedicated/private?
[01:28] Diego Ramos: Sure. High-level: hosted is fast to start and we optimize routing and caching. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and predictable latency at scale. Private/VPC gives you the control for keys and data residency. For streaming specifically, we have continuous batching and an async path for chunk emission which reduces tail latency, plus prefix/KV cache to shave early tokens. But there are tradeoffs — if your bursts are very spiky, dedicated with autoscaling plus burst capacity avoids noisy neighbor issues.
[01:58] Priya Nair: We're regulatory-heavy so private is attractive, but cost and ops are concerns. Our security folks will want KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, SSO with our IDP.
[02:10] Diego Ramos: We support KMS integration for key wrapping, audit logs, and SAML SSO. For private deployments we can run a control plane with customer-managed network.
[02:22] Liam O'Reilly: For benchmarking, we currently have traces — we can provide traffic captures and p95 targets. What should we run as baseline test?
[02:30] Diego Ramos: Ideally a 24-hour trace replay which includes the bursts. Baseline plan: run a steady-state 1-hour at average concurrency, then a 6-hour with repeated burst windows, then a 24-hour continuous replay to capture diurnal patterns. We'd measure p50/p90/p95/p99 latency for chunk emission and token/sec throughput per GPU.
[02:48] Priya Nair: How do quantization and model variants affect p95 and token/sec? We might want an 8-bit quantized model in dedicated to save cost.
[02:58] Diego Ramos: Quantization usually reduces memory and can increase throughput but might affect quality. We have recommended quantization profiles per model family. For p95, quantization helps reduce kernel time; combined with larger batch windows it improves token/sec but sometimes adds jitter on very short sequences. We can run side-by-side comparisons in the benchmark.
[03:20] Sara Gomez: Any known pitfall with KV cache for streaming? Our streams often have long conversations, cache hit rates vary.
[03:28] Diego Ramos: KV cache helps a lot for repeated prefixes but if sequences are highly divergent the hit rate drops; the runtime manages KV eviction based on sequence length distribution. For long tails, we recommend pinning model versions and configuring cache retention accordingly.
[03:42] Liam O'Reilly: Can Redwood route by policy? For example, fall back to a cheaper quantized model during overloads?
[03:50] Maya Chen: Yes — smart routing supports policies by latency/cost/region and automatic fallback to compatible model variants. We can also set graceful degradation, e.g., shorter context or quantized variant.
[03:59] Priya Nair: On observability, what telemetry will we get? Token-level cost? Traces?
[04:08] Diego Ramos: Console has token-level cost, per-route latency histograms, traces and error analysis. We can emit traces to your OTLP endpoint and provide logs for auditing.
[04:18] Liam O'Reilly: For the burst scenario, what's realistic token/sec per GPU for our model family? We're using an LLaMA-style 13B.
[04:27] Diego Ramos: For an optimized 13B on A-architecture GPUs (our dedicated profiles), you might see sustained token/sec anywhere from 300 to 1k tokens/sec per GPU depending on quantization and sequence length. Short token/chunk streaming favors higher tokens/sec but p95 depends on tail behavior.
[04:45] Priya Nair: That seems like a range. We'll need concrete numbers from a benchmark using our trace, otherwise our cost model is fuzzy.
[04:53] Maya Chen: We'll own the benchmark setup. Diego will send a test plan and a runner you can execute or we can run in hosted sandbox. Which do you prefer?
[05:02] Liam O'Reilly: Prefer that Redwood runs an initial hosted sandbox run against our trace so we avoid onion setup. If results look good we'll discuss dedicated sizing.
[05:11] Priya Nair: One more thing: p95 failure modes — if you miss p95 by, say, 40ms occasionally, do you have automated fallbacks?
[05:21] Diego Ramos: We have automatic fallback policies at the routing layer and can divert to a lower-latency region, or swap to a model variant. Also configure admission control to shed lower-priority requests during extreme bursts.
[05:34] Sara Gomez: About multi-tenant isolation — in hosted mode, do you provide per-tenant resource caps? We're concerned about noisy neighbors.
[05:42] Diego Ramos: Yes, rate limits and quotas per token/embedding, plus model-level limits. For high isolation you should look at Dedicated or Private. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and better predictability.
[05:55] Liam O'Reilly: Pricing wise, what's the delta between hosted and dedicated for a workload that averages 150M tokens/day with big bursts?
[06:04] Maya Chen: We'll send a detailed priced matrix but high level: hosted is usage-based — good for variable traffic; Dedicated is a capacity reservation with lower unit costs at steady high volumes plus burst options; private has an additional platform fee and infra ops cost. We'll include examples in the pricing sheet.
[06:20] Priya Nair: Security review — we need SOC 2 type II and ISO docs. Also can you integrate with our HSM for key storage in private?
[06:29] Diego Ramos: Yes to SOC2 docs we can share, and for private we support KMS/HSM keywrap or bring-your-own-key patterns. We'll include those artifacts.
[06:38] Liam O'Reilly: For the benchmark runner, what metrics will you capture exactly?
[06:43] Diego Ramos: We'll capture p50/p90/p95/p99 for chunk emission and end-to-end, tokens/sec per GPU, GPU utilization, kernel times, memory usage, KV cache hit/miss rates, and failure/error rates. We'll also correlate cost.
[06:59] Priya Nair: Great. Any suggested initial p95 SLO we should aim for based on what you heard?
[07:05] Maya Chen: From what you've given, aiming for chunk p95 <= 200ms is reasonable in hosted, and dedicated should be able to hit <= 150ms with proper sizing and quantization. We'll validate in the benchmark.
[07:16] Liam O'Reilly: Okay, can you also include guidance on autoscaling policies and burst pre-warming? We saw cold-start spikes in our initial tests.
[07:26] Diego Ramos: Absolutely — we'll recommend autoscaling configs and pre-warming suggestions; for streamed workloads, maintaining a warm pool for a predictable burst window helps. We'll include configuration snippets.
[07:36] Priya Nair: About routing — can we have region-based routing plus fallback to a second region? We need multi-region failover for continuity.
[07:44] Diego Ramos: Yes, smart routing supports region preference with automatic failover. We can set priority regions and fallback tiers.
[07:51] Maya Chen: Quick note — competitors like VendorX advertise similar autoscaling but with less KV cache and less transparent cost breakdown, which we've seen cause surprises.
[07:59] Priya Nair: Noted. Any compliance or procurement gating items we should prepare?
[08:05] Maya Chen: We'll send a procurement checklist: SOC2 docs, ATO info, SSO configs, and procurement contact details.
[08:12] Liam O'Reilly: One last question for Diego: If we go private on-prem, what's the typical deployment time and ops footprint?
[08:19] Diego Ramos: On-prem packages typically take 4–8 weeks for initial deployment depending on networking and HSM integration. We'll provide an ops runbook and optional managed services. For VPC it's quicker, usually 2–3 weeks.
[08:32] Maya Chen: Okay, let's recap next steps before we close.
[08:36] Priya Nair: Quick thing — can we include a stress scenario where we simulate a 10x burst for 30 seconds? That's one of our worst-case tests.
[08:45] Diego Ramos: Yes we'll include that in the benchmark plan as an extreme spike test to validate admission control and fallback latency.
[08:52] Maya Chen: Recap and owners: Maya to send pricing and procurement checklist; Diego to send benchmark plan and run hosted sandbox on your trace; Liam to provide traces and p95 targets; all to reconvene after initial benchmark.
[09:06] Priya Nair: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:09] Maya Chen: Thanks all. We'll follow up by Friday with artifacts.

(Transcript truncated for brevity; full call includes technical deep dive and some screen-share notes on benchmark tool configuration.)

End of meeting.
